incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using deepfake videos and fake social media profiles featuring his likeness to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals promote fraudulent immigration services, including offering US residency assistance for $2,200 to undocumented immigrants without deportation orders. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, and he estimates the problem has grown dramatically in recent months.

To combat the fraud, Leal hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scams typically direct victims through social media videos to contact numbers via WhatsApp, where fraudsters send phony contracts and request payment through apps like Venmo and Zelle. Leal is warning immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to avoid anyone requesting immediate payment. He plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scammers' origins.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article claimed Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article and interview never actually occurred. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated, according to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. Scammers use artificial intelligence to create deepfake images and videos of well-known Australians to promote fraudulent investments.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase from the previous year, with phishing scams jumping 279 percent and fake investment platforms rising 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, businesswoman Gina Rinehart, and finance presenter Alan Kohler are among the most commonly impersonated public figures. Scammers build elaborate fake websites, news articles, and reviews to deceive consumers into providing personal information and money. ASIC advises people to verify financial licenses through official registers before investing and not to trust investment opportunities based solely on celebrity endorsements.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A class-action lawsuit has been filed against Oura, the smart ring company, accusing it of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit, filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco on Thursday, alleges that Oura's rings cannot accurately measure sleep stages despite marketing claims suggesting they can detect what only hospital sleep labs can see. The rings cost $300 and up, and the company claims an 11 billion dollar valuation built on consumer trust. The lawsuit contends that Oura's algorithms and sensors lack the ability to detect physiological signals needed for accurate sleep stage measurement and instead rely on unreliable artificial intelligence estimates comparable to guessing.

Oura disputes the allegations, stating it stands behind its science and accuracy claims, noting that its rings use multiple physiological signals like heart rate and breathing patterns. The company acknowledged that its products are not medical devices but said independent studies have validated its sleep staging against clinical standards. The suit seeks class action status and a jury trial, though it remains unclear what compensation customers might receive if the lawsuit succeeds. This marks another legal challenge for Oura, which is already facing a separate class action over allegedly collecting personal information without consent.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The attackers deployed a custom ransomware called encrypt.out that uses ChaCha20 encryption and can selectively encrypt virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation across ten target organizations. The agent performed tasks including network scanning, domain enumeration, and NTLM relay attacks, with strict restrictions imposed by operators against DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding new computer objects to domains.

Researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity affecting eight victim organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This second group used different techniques including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. Aurora operates a data leak site and demands ransom through a Tor portal, with victims receiving access keys after their files are encrypted. The investigation provided indicators of compromise including multiple IP addresses, URLs, and file hashes to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware attacks.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Chaac Pizza Northeast, a major Pizza Hut franchisee operating approximately 111 locations across the Northeast, filed a lawsuit in Texas Business Court on May 6 claiming that Pizza Hut's mandatory adoption of Dragontail, an AI-powered delivery management system, caused over $100 million in damages. The franchisee alleges that after the 2024 rollout, the system gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations, causing drivers to wait up to 15 minutes to batch multiple orders together instead of immediately delivering completed pizzas. This resulted in significantly slower deliveries and reduced customer satisfaction, while also allowing drivers to see tip amounts and payment methods, making them less likely to accept certain orders.

Before Dragontail's implementation, Chaac maintained over 90% on-time delivery within 30 minutes and achieved double-digit sales growth with above-average customer satisfaction scores. Following the rollout, performance deteriorated sharply, with New York City year-over-year sales swinging from positive 10.19% to negative 9.78%. Chaac claims Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training or support and ignored worsening metrics. The franchisee is seeking over $100 million in damages plus attorneys' fees. Pizza Hut stated it would respond through appropriate legal channels but declined further comment.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and "Fresh Air" staff members to trick authors, entertainers, and other public figures into paying fees for fake interview opportunities. The fraudulent emails are highly personalized, referencing victims' recent work and proposing interview topics to appear legitimate. One target, Misericordia University history professor Jennifer Black, initially received what seemed like an exciting invitation but grew suspicious when asked to pay $250 for production costs. She called WHYY to verify and confirmed the email was fraudulent.

According to cybersecurity experts, artificial intelligence has made these traditional impersonation scams more convincing and affordable for criminals to execute. Similar schemes have targeted comedians and journalists. WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating the matter. The organizations emphasized they never charge guests for interviews and that any requests for payment should be considered illegitimate. Experts recommend verifying requests through official channels and noting red flags like personal email addresses or requests for money.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for AI chatbots. The website presents pro-Israel arguments on topics including Palestinian torture, Israeli war crimes, and Gaza starvation as neutral research, with all headlines formatted as questions users might ask chatbots. The New York production company Piro Inc filed the operation with the US Justice Department as Israeli government propaganda material. The institute claims no legal existence, has no physical address or named staff, and initially denied external funding before later contradicting that statement.

The campaign is part of a broader Israeli government effort, financed by tens of millions of dollars through the European advertising group Havas Media, aimed at influencing artificial intelligence systems to promote Israel's position. Israeli officials have privately expressed frustration that the expensive public diplomacy campaign has failed, with American support for Israel significantly declining. Recent polling shows 36 percent of Americans sympathize with Israel, down from higher levels, and 60 percent view Israel unfavorably as of April 2026.

incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Atlantic Records, and Capitol Records, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular artificial intelligence music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission and directly reproducing sections of famous songs in their generated outputs. The record labels claim the companies deliberately concealed which songs they used to train their models and falsely argued their practices constitute fair use.

To support their case, the record labels created specific prompts and demonstrated they could generate songs that closely replicate works from artists including The Beatles, The Beach Boys, Frank Sinatra, Chuck Berry, Michael Jackson, and Mariah Carey. Examples include an Udio-generated song that copies Green Day's "American Idiot" and a Suno-generated track nearly identical to "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, and the record labels submitted a thumb drive containing examples of infringing AI-generated music alongside a list of thousands of allegedly scraped copyrighted works.

incidents.title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio
incidents.summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. The settlement includes licensing agreements between the two companies. UMG and other major record labels had sued Udio for allegedly using hit songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission to create similar AI-generated music. Under the new deal, Udio will launch a platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, create, stream and share songs. The financial terms were not disclosed.

This marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label and represents a shift in how the AI music industry may operate going forward. Udio CEO Andrew Sanchez stated the collaboration demonstrates how AI and the music industry can work together to support artists. Artists can choose to participate in the new platform and will receive compensation, though specific details were not provided. Udio, which launched in 2024 and has been used by millions of people, was co-founded by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by notable investors including will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized after artificial intelligence generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in court filings related to a Los Angeles homeowner's lawsuit. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire made her Carson home uninhabitable, followed by water damage during repairs. She claimed delays in getting insurance approval prevented completion of reconstruction work, leading her family to drain savings and retirement accounts, declare bankruptcy, and lose their home to foreclosure. A lawyer named Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare the motions, incorrectly believing it would check citations accurately.

The firm Musick, Peeler & Garrett, which represents State Farm, acknowledged seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized and said the firm updated its AI policies. State Farm said it expects external counsel to meet the highest ethical standards. The case is scheduled for trial in October. AI hallucinations in legal work have become increasingly common as the legal industry adopts generative AI tools, with one database tracking nearly 2,000 such cases worldwide.

stories.Headline: Electoral court sets new standards for AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Brazil's highest electoral court established new guidelines for identifying artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes in political content ahead of October elections. The ruling came from a case involving opposition candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who displayed AI-created images of his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, at his party's convention in July. The deepfake showed the former president endorsing his son's campaign against current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to lead a coup.

The court voted 4-3 to not punish Senator Bolsonaro, determining the deepfake was shown at a private party event rather than a public political advertisement. However, the court voted 5-2 to formally define what constitutes a deepfake in political advertising as synthetic content created or altered using artificial intelligence technology that realistically reproduces a person's image, voice, or speech. These standards will apply to thousands of campaign ads broadcasters must air before the October 4 election, during 14 minutes of daily airtime designated for political commercials.

stories.Headline: Datametrex Plans to Focus on AI, Data Centre, and Patent Licensing
stories.Summary:
Datametrex AI Limited announced plans to shut down its healthcare operations to focus on artificial intelligence, data centre technology, and patent licensing. The company operates medical clinics in Edmonton, Calgary, and Vancouver, British Columbia, providing primary and emergency care services. The gradual wind-down aims to streamline the corporate structure, reduce operating costs and regulatory requirements, and improve financial performance by redirecting resources toward core business areas.

The company will manage the transition carefully, considering operational, financial, contractual, and regulatory factors. Management plans to assess opportunities to maximize value from healthcare assets during the process. The strategic shift allows Datametrex to concentrate capital and resources on artificial intelligence and data centre initiatives, which align with long-term objectives. The company indicated it would provide further updates as developments occur.

stories.Headline: FG, IFAD, stakeholders push AI-enabled extension to transform Nigeria's agriculture
stories.Summary:
# Summary

The Federal Government, International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), and other organizations are working to introduce artificial intelligence-powered digital extension services to help Nigerian farmers. At a workshop in Abuja, stakeholders committed to using this technology to deliver timely agricultural advice tailored to individual farmers' locations, crops, weather conditions, and market opportunities. The IFAD country director emphasized that AI-enabled extension is crucial for transforming Nigeria's agricultural policies into practical services that improve food security and support climate resilience.

The initiative addresses a critical shortage of agricultural extension workers in Nigeria, where the ratio of one extension agent to between 5,000 and 10,000 farmers far exceeds the recommended benchmark of one agent per 800 to 1,000 farmers. A pilot program in Kano and Ogun States has already registered nearly 21,000 farmers through the FarmerChat AI platform, which provides weather updates and pest guidance in multiple languages. However, challenges including limited smartphone ownership, internet connectivity issues, and low digital literacy must be addressed for wider adoption.

stories.Headline: Protein Industries Canada invests in AI technology to boost on-farm productivity and bring new solutions to farmers
stories.Summary:
Protein Industries Canada is investing $4.9 million into two artificial intelligence projects designed to help Canadian farmers increase productivity and improve safety. The projects involve partnerships between companies like TerraVision360, Metos Canada, Rocky Mountain Equipment, Super GeoAI Technology Inc., and Southview Farms. The first project will create an AI tool to predict and manage disease risk in pulse crops by analyzing weather and crop data, enabling farmers to apply fungicides more strategically and reduce costs. The second project will develop a drone and LiDAR system to measure grain volumes in storage bins accurately while eliminating the need for dangerous manual climbing.

These investments are part of Canada's effort to advance agricultural innovation and support the adoption of made-in-Canada AI solutions. Government officials emphasized that the projects will strengthen farm competitiveness, reduce operational risks, and enhance worker safety across the agriculture sector. The funding comes through the Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy and supports the broader goal of growing Canada's plant-based food and ingredient industry to $25 billion.

stories.Headline: USF Faculty Split on AI Use in Classrooms
stories.Summary:
University of South Florida held a panel discussion Monday where faculty members debated whether artificial intelligence should be embraced, adapted to, or resisted in classroom settings. John Licato, an associate professor in the Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, and Stephanie Arthur, an assistant professor in the College of Education, both support using AI tools. They argue that AI is already present in students' lives and can help with personalized learning and language support. Licato noted that AI can save students time and money on projects, while Arthur emphasized the importance of building AI literacy early, even starting with first graders.

Deepak Singh, a writing instructor at the Judy Genshaft Honors College, disagreed strongly. He believes AI undermines human creativity and intelligence, arguing that students should create work through their own effort rather than relying on machines. Singh also contends that students who learn without AI assistance retain more information. The faculty acknowledged that some concerns exist, including the potential for AI to replace meaningful human interaction and feedback necessary for learning.
